data.title: US yields climb, but 10-year holds under 5% as AI jitters linger
data.description:
Key points:
  • Yields higher after tumble in the prior session
  • S&P Composite PMI eases to 57.6
  • Two-year yield on pace for fourth straight week of declines

By Chuck Mikolajczak

US Treasury yields rose on Friday, a day after the benchmark 10-year yield saw its biggest one-day drop in nearly four years, but remained under the 5% mark as concerns about the durability of a rally in AI-related stocks lingered.

The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note rose 3.7 basis points to 4.99%. The 10-year yield is down about 11 basis points on the week and on pace for a third straight week of declines, its longest run lower since June.

Investors have shifted toward safer assets such as government debt on recent concerns about the sustainability of the AI trade, a major component of the current bull market for equities. The bond market's recent rally has come even as economic data point to continued price pressures and oil prices have advanced above $100 per barrel.

But while the S&P 500 technology sector was higher as AI fears cooled, the broader S&P 500 CBOE:SPX retreated.

The 10-year yield plunged 19.3 basis points on Thursday, its biggest drop since March 10, 2023, when SVB Financial Group was closed by regulators after the bank's failed attempt to raise capital.

"We're going to see yields over 5% for the 10-year again. We're not that far away, but this is not like, 'oh, okay, we're off to the races here,'" said JoAnne Bianco, partner and senior investment strategist at BondBloxx Investment Management in Chicago.

"There are still all these headwinds in terms of sticky inflation, growing Treasury supply to finance the deficits, just the need in general, with all the uncertainty that we have for higher term premiums and then higher energy prices that seem to be here to stay for a while."

COMPOSITE INDEX SLIPS FROM PEAK

Yields rose further after S&P Global said its flash US Composite PMI Output Index, which tracks the manufacturing and services sectors, slipped to 57.6 this month from a five-year-high of 58.4 in September, though it remained well above the 50 threshold that signals expansion.

The yield on the 30-year bond (US30YT=RR) added 2.9 basis points to 5.316%, but was down nearly 13 basis points on the week, also on track for a third straight week of declines.

Even as economic data points to rising price pressures, market expectations for a rate increase from the Federal Reserve at its policy meeting next week have wilted. The probability of a hike of at least 25 basis points has shrunk to 9.4%, according to CME FedWatch, from 15.5% a week ago and 70.9% a month earlier.

A closely watched part of the US Treasury yield curve measuring the gap between yields on 2- and 10-year Treasury notes (US2US10=TWEB), seen as an indicator of economic expectations, was at a positive 29.6 basis points.

The University of Michigan's Surveys of Consumers showed its Consumer Sentiment Index dropped to 48.0 this month from a final reading of 48.1 in September.

The 2-year (US2YT=RR) US Treasury yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Fed, climbed 5.5 basis points to 4.69%, putting it down about 5 basis points on the week, which would be a fourth consecutive week of declines, its longest stretch of the year.

The breakeven rate on 5-year US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) (US5YTIP=TWEB) was last at 2.456%, on track for its highest close since September 10, after closing at 2.38% on Thursday.

The 10-year TIPS breakeven rate (US10YTIP=TWEB) was last at 2.346%, indicating the market sees inflation averaging about 2.3% a year for the next decade.

data.title: Moderna Executives Sold Shares in Trades Planned Before Vaccine Results — WSJ
data.description:
By Theo Francis

Two Moderna executives sold more than $30 million in shares in the weeks after a closely watched cancer vaccine study triggered a surge in the stock price-and before more detailed results reversed some of the gains, securities filings show.

The sales by Chief Financial Officer James Mock and President Stephen Hoge were made under pre-set trading plans the men adopted in June. That was a couple months before Moderna's shares more than doubled Aug. 19, when it announced its mRNA-based vaccine had prevented melanoma from returning or spreading.

Hoge sold nearly $27 million in shares in mid-September and mid-October after exercising options scheduled to expire in February. Both times, he kept close to half the shares received from the options, valued at about $25 million at the time. Mock sold $2 million in shares received by exercising stock options and another $2 million in other shares on Sept. 10. The executives' share sales were at prices ranging from $134 to $217.

Moderna shares fell nearly 18% Thursday after details from the cancer-vaccine study were shared on social media, raising concerns the treatment might not be as effective as initially hoped.

The sales look routine, said Ben Silverman, head of research at VerityData, which tracks insider stock transactions for investors. Moderna shares were trading around $50 when the executives adopted the trading plans in June, and most of the sales came before the stock's significant run-up in October.

This item is part of a Wall Street Journal live coverage event. The full stream can be found by searching P/WSJL (WSJ Live Coverage).

data.title: CBOT corn weakens as harvest advances
data.description:
Chicago Board of Trade corn futures eased on Friday as the harvest advanced in the US Midwest and traders positioned ahead of the weekend, according to analysts.

  • Dry weather conditions have been beneficial for harvesting in the US Midwest this week, but showers are expected to expand across the region next week, according to Commodity Weather Group.

  • Analysts said market players were attempting to minimize its headline risk ahead of the weekend, creating lackluster trade.

  • Some US farmers were finishing their soybean harvest after a stretch of favorable Midwest weather and were shifting to harvesting corn, according to analysts.

  • The US Department of Agriculture confirmed private sales of 116,000 metric tons of US corn to unknown destinations.

data.title: Dell Stocks Rise 2.1% as New AI Systems Face a 2027 Delivery Test
data.description:
AI-systems supplier Dell Technologies expanded its Nvidia hardware lineup, with shares at $462.51, up approximately 2.12%, at 11:30 a.m. ET on October 23. The rollout gives investors two timelines to watch. According to Data Center Dynamics, the smaller Vera CPU server arrives this month, while the Vera rack and Groq 3 inference system are scheduled for the first quarter of 2027. The products broaden Dell's AI offering, but some of the shipping opportunity sits next year. DCD

Demand is building. Dell said its AI Factory with Nvidia now serves more than 6,500 customers, compared with 5,000 last quarteran increase exceeding 30%. Its preceding earnings release reported $60.9 billion in AI-server orders, $16.4 billion in AI-server revenue and a $95 billion ending backlog. That backlog represents roughly 5.8 times the quarter's AI-server revenue. It signals substantial business to fulfill, without telling investors exactly when those orders become sales. investors.delltechnologies.com

The valuation raises the stakes: Dell trades 91.39% above the $241.66 GF Value estimate, leaving a substantial premium against that benchmark. Customer growth helps explain the enthusiasm. Protecting that enthusiasm takes execution. Dell needs to meet launch dates, turn orders into shipments and preserve margins along the way. Cash conversion matters, too. Rising inventory and receivables can soak up cash even while revenue accelerates. The next test is how much profitable cash Dell can generate from the demand already on its books.

data.title: CoreWeave Faces New Test as UBS Defends AI Bull Case
data.description:
CoreWeave shares continued to slide Friday even as UBS reiterated its bullish stance on the AI infrastructure company, underscoring how difficult the current setup has become for heavily leveraged AI names.

UBS kept a Buy rating on CoreWeave while cutting its price target to $105 from $120, according to Investing.com.

The stock has been under sustained pressure as investors question whether the enormous amount of debt and capital required to build AI infrastructure can generate sufficient long-term returns.

Those concerns have intensified as interest rates remain elevated and financing costs climb across the sector.

CoreWeave is particularly exposed because its growth model depends on aggressively adding GPU capacity while carrying a large debt load.

BofA recently reiterated a Buy rating and $140 target, but estimated that CoreWeave may still need roughly $20 billion in additional funding to serve its contracted demand. The firm also highlighted the company's roughly $129 billion in remaining performance obligations.

That backlog is the core of the bullish case.

Demand for AI compute remains extremely strong, and UBS has previously argued that the market is underestimating both the durability of that demand and CoreWeave's ability to monetize each gigawatt of capacity.

UBS analyst Karl Keirstead previously estimated that revenue per gigawatt could rise from roughly $11 billion today to more than $15 billion over time as GPU pricing remains firm.

But the bearish case is equally clear.

CoreWeave remains highly leveraged, customer concentration is substantial, and higher interest rates make every incremental dollar of infrastructure more expensive to finance.

That tension has become the defining issue for the stock.

Investor Takeaway

I think CoreWeave is becoming one of the clearest tests of whether the AI infrastructure boom can survive higher financing costs.

The demand is real.

The backlog is massive.

But investors are no longer willing to ignore the balance sheet.

That is why a bullish UBS call is not enough by itself to reverse the stock's decline.

For investors, the key things to watch are funding costs, bond yields, capacity additions, backlog conversion, free cash flow, and whether CoreWeave can improve leverage faster than it adds new infrastructure.

The bull case is still built around constrained AI compute supply.

The market is simply demanding much more proof that the economics work.

data.title: Micron Stocks Rise 3.41% as $1,700 Target Puts Cash Durability in Focus
data.description:
Memory producer Micron rose 3.41% to $885.685 at 11.30 a.m. ET on October 23, as investors weighed BNP Paribas's $1,700 price target. According to Barron's, analyst Karl Ackerman maintained his Buy rating and highlighted memory constraints in AI inference. That target implies roughly 91.9% upside. The hurdle is clear: Micron needs to keep turning tight supply into cash.

The cash engine is already running hard. Micron reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $54.23 billion and operating cash flow of $43.97 billion. Net capital investment consumed $10.77 billion, leaving adjusted free cash flow of $33.20 billionabout 61.2% of revenue. Those numbers give the bullish case substance. Keeping that cash conversion strong as investment climbs is the next test.

The valuation picture adds a reality check: shares trade 11.04% above the $797.62 GF Value estimate, suggesting some optimism is already priced in. AI demand can keep memory shipments growing, but more capacity could pressure pricing. Watch selling prices, shipment growth and capital spending together. One exceptional quarter supports the story; sustained cash generation has to carry the valuation.

data.title: Netflix Hits a 52-Week Low as Valuation Gets Cheaper
data.description:
Netflix Inc. (NFLX, Financials) is reaching a new 52-week low as investors weigh slower growth versus a much cheaper valuation.

The business is trading at around 17 times expected profits, which some analysts deem attractive on a historical value basis. The firm's doing well.

Third quarter revenues as projected, operating margin of 34.6% Churn also improved despite price rises, and Netflix bought back a record $4.8 billion of its stock. The problem is growth.

Its projection for the fourth quarter suggests a further fall and cut its outlook for advertising revenue by around 10%.

There's also more rivalry, with outlets like YouTube and the combined Skydance-HBO Max-Paramount+ company battling over viewers.

The conversation among investors now is less about whether Netflix is a solid company and more about how much growth is required to make the stock worth it.

Large margins and buybacks might signal Netflix doesn't need prior growth to make shareholder value. Next up to watch: how advertising and subscription patterns play out during the fourth quarter.

data.title: Euro sinks on French debt worries, yen gains for week on AI rout
data.description:
Key points:
  • Euro drops on concerns over French unrest, Moody's rating decision awaited
  • Japanese yen benefits from safe-haven flow after AI rout
  • US dollar index to end week little changed

By Karen Brettell

The euro fell on Friday and was on track for a weekly loss against both the US dollar and the yen as a selloff in French government bonds pushed the country's debt risk premium to its highest level since the euro zone sovereign debt crisis in 2011.

The Japanese yen was headed for a weekly increase against the greenback as it benefited from safe-haven flows from the selloff in AI stocks on Thursday. The dollar index was little changed on the week.

The euro was hit by concerns about growing unrest in France and the country's worsening budget problems. France will deploy 70,000 police backed by specialist units for protests on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said. The country also faces the threat of a rating downgrade by Moody’s on Friday.

"The pressure in the European bond market has eased today, but Moody’s review of France’s debt rating late today poses a challenge, and although the Macron government has threatened military assistance to quell the social unrest, more activity is likely this weekend," said Marc Chandler, chief market strategist at Bannockburn Global Forex.

The euro was last down 0.21% at $1.1191 , set to end the week 0.43% lower. It fell more sharply against the yen, touching its lowest level since October 2025 at 175.08 yen . It was last down 0.11% against the Japanese currency and on track for a weekly decline of 1.1%.

The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.25% to 101.82 and was headed for a weekly gain of 0.03%.

The yen weakened 0.1% to 156.9 per dollar and was on track for a weekly gain of around 0.7%, its best week since mid-September.

"The yen has continued to trade at stronger levels at the end of this week, encouraged by more risk-off trading conditions," said Lee Hardman, senior currency analyst at MUFG.

CENTRAL BANK POLICY MEETINGS IN FOCUS

Traders are looking to next week's policy meetings at the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan. All three are expected to leave rates unchanged, but investors will look for clues on the future path of policy.

Fed funds futures traders trimmed bets on a December hike after Thursday's stock market selloff, though they still see an 81% chance of such a move, according to LSEG data.

Traders see a 66% chance of an ECB hike in December. Investors will scrutinize any hint of the rate outlook after ECB President Christine Lagarde said in late September that a moderate policy response to inflation was appropriate.

Purchasing Managers' Index data showed private-sector growth in the euro zone slowed in October to its weakest pace in four months, hurt by a renewed contraction in France.

"The drop brings the PMIs back in line with other growth indicators, in our view, rather than suggesting downside risks from here," Giada Giani, an economist at Citi, said. "France remains a drag, but the rest of the euro area remains resilient."

In Japan, data on Friday showed annual core consumer inflation exceeded the central bank's 2% target in September for the first time in nine months. The reading points to broadening price pressures and strengthens the case for a near-term rate hike, analysts said.

Traders are pricing in 61% odds of a BOJ hike in December.

data.title: Norwegian Cruise Faces New Warning on 2027 Recovery
data.description:
Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings was downgraded to Underweight from Neutral at JPMorgan ahead of its upcoming earnings report, with the bank warning that the cruise operator's expected yield recovery could prove weaker than investors expect.

JPMorgan also cut its price target to $11, reflecting a more cautious outlook for 2027.

Analyst Matthew Boss expects third-quarter net yields to fall 7.9%, roughly in line with Wall Street and better than management's guidance for an 8.9% decline. He forecasts EPS of $0.93, slightly ahead of the $0.90 consensus, and expects Norwegian to reaffirm its full-year 2026 outlook.

The bigger concern is what comes next.

JPMorgan models flat constant-currency net yield growth in 2027, below the Street's roughly 0.8% expectation. The bank sees yields falling 5.3% in the first quarter before improving to 3.2% growth in the back half of the year.

Even that recovery could prove too optimistic.

Boss warned that prolonged geopolitical pressures could make it harder for Norwegian to recapture demand in Europe. Roughly 85% of Norwegian's European itineraries are sourced from U.S.-based customers, the highest exposure in JPMorgan's cruise coverage.

Costs are another problem.

JPMorgan expects adjusted net cruise costs excluding fuel to rise 1.8% in 2027, versus the Street's 0.9% estimate. That would still sit below management's stated goal of keeping expense growth under the current 3% to 3.5% inflation rate, but it leaves less room for margin recovery.

Norwegian has already acknowledged demand pressure.

Its second-quarter filing said bookings remained below the company's optimal position for the next 12 months, citing softer Norwegian Cruise Line demand, company-specific execution issues and the conflict in the Middle East.

Investor Takeaway

I think the most important part of JPMorgan's downgrade is that the bank is not especially worried about the upcoming quarter.

It is worried about how quickly Norwegian can recover in 2027.

The company may still beat or meet near-term expectations, but if yields remain weak while costs rise faster than Wall Street expects, the earnings recovery could be much slower than the market is pricing in.

Geopolitical risk makes that setup even tougher because Norwegian has unusually high exposure to U.S. customers booking European itineraries.

For investors, the key things to watch are 2027 yield guidance, booking curves, Europe demand, fuel costs and whether management can keep expense growth below inflation.

The downgrade is essentially a warning that the recovery may take longer and cost more than expected.

data.title: Blackstone Sees Massive AI Demand Despite Bubble Concerns
data.description:
Blackstone President Jon Gray is pushing back against mounting fears that artificial intelligence investment is becoming a bubble, arguing that demand is already running far ahead of supply.

Gray said the current AI buildout looks very different from past bubbles because companies are not building infrastructure first and simply hoping customers eventually arrive.

When you think about a bubble, you think about building capacity and then hoping the demand comes, Gray said in an interview with Bloomberg. With AI, you're building capacity, and you're hoping you can keep up with the demand.

Gray said spending on AI models across Blackstone portfolio companies has increased about 20-fold year over year.

He also pointed to Ode, an AI deployment company created by Blackstone and Anthropic, saying the business is struggling to keep up with customer demand.

Demand is almost parabolic, Gray said.

The bigger constraint, in Blackstone's view, remains supply.

Gray highlighted bottlenecks around power, chips, permitting and capital, which are making it difficult to bring new compute capacity online quickly enough. Blackstone has focused heavily on that infrastructure layer, including data centers and energy assets contracted to major technology companies.

His comments come as the AI bubble debate intensifies.

Citadel founder Ken Griffin recently argued that investors are almost certainly in an AI bubble, while global credit markets have also shown growing unease over the amount of debt being used to fund AI infrastructure.

Investor takeaway

I think Gray's argument gets to the heart of the AI bubble debate.The question is not whether spending is enormous. It clearly is.The question is whether that spending is running ahead of demand.

Blackstone's answer is no.

Gray's point is that companies are scrambling to build enough infrastructure to satisfy customers who already want more compute, rather than constructing speculative capacity with no obvious end user.

That is a meaningful distinction from the 1990s telecom bubble.

But it does not eliminate every risk.

Even if AI demand remains strong, investors still have to ask whether individual projects can earn enough to cover financing costs, depreciation and massive upfront capital requirements.

For investors, the key things to watch are compute utilization, power availability, AI model spending, data-center financing and whether hyperscalers can turn rapidly rising capex into sustainable cash returns.

The demand may be real.

The debate is increasingly about whether the economics will be just as strong.

data.title: American Express Makes Major Cost Move Despite Strong Earnings
data.description:
American Express plans to cut about 5% of its global workforce as the payments giant looks to become more efficient and agile amid rising costs.

Chairman and CEO Stephen Squeri told analysts after the company's third-quarter earnings that the reductions are designed to remove organizational layers and speed up decision-making, according to Bloomberg.

With American Express employing roughly 78,000 people, a 5% reduction would translate to around 3,500 jobs.

The move comes despite a relatively strong earnings report.

American Express reported third-quarter adjusted EPS of $4.68, beating Wall Street expectations, and raised its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to $17.60 to $17.90.

Still, investors focused on slower network-volume growth compared with the second quarter, helping send the stock down about 2.4% in premarket trading.

The layoffs also fit into a broader cost-cutting trend across financial services.

Barclays recently announced around 5,000 job reductions, while HSBC has outlined plans to reduce staffing across parts of its U.K. wealth-management business.

Some banks have increasingly linked workforce reductions to automation and artificial intelligence, although American Express framed its own move primarily around efficiency, agility and reducing layers.

Investor Takeaway

I think the important part of this story is the timing.

American Express is not cutting jobs because earnings collapsed.

It is doing so while raising its profit outlook, which suggests management is trying to protect margins before cost pressures become a bigger problem.

That can be positive if the company removes bureaucracy without hurting customer service, cardmember growth or spending volumes.

But investors should still pay attention to the softer network-volume trend.

For investors, the key things to watch are expense growth, network volumes, credit quality, employee-related savings and whether the restructuring helps American Express expand margins into 2027.

data.title: Crude Oil Skyrockets Amid Rising Supply Concerns Due To Dual Middle East Tensions
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - Crude oil prices have catapulted on Friday both due to increasing fears of a fresh, deep and intense U.S.-Iran war as well as the ongoing Houthi-Saudi Arabia conflict. The escalation could result in halting the oil and energy flows from the Arab nations for a protracted period of time.

WTI Crude Oil for December delivery was last seen trading up by $3.54 (or 3.56%) at $103.01 per barrel.

The fears of renewed escalation in the Middle East that surfaced since yesterday continued to dictate crude oil prices.

Yesterday, the New York Times reported that the U.S. and Israel are preparing to conduct joint military attacks on Iran.

The strikes are reportedly slated to be launched anytime after the midterm elections in the U.S. in the first week of November are over. The operation could target Iran's nuclear installations, energy infrastructure, and missile and drone facilities.

However, the report did not rule out scope for negotiations and mentioned that talks with Iran are ongoing.

In South Carolina, Trump stated that though U.S. forces could start returning back to the U.S. as Iran has been weakened militarily and financially, he preferred to reach a durable solution to all the issues that started the conflict rather than striking a temporary peace deal.

Earlier, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps announced that it is all set to unveil a new weapon, which the military termed as the 'Father Of All Bombs,' to combat any sophisticated attacks by U.S. forces.

A couple of days before, the Wall Street Journal reported that Persian Gulf oil exports have crossed pre-war levels including shipments through Hormuz and other alternative routes, aided by the U.S. protection despite Iran's attacks.

The flows averaged more than 24 million barrels a day for the week through October 18.

Through Truth Social, Trump tagged the report to support his claim that the U.S. is winning the war.

Trump also accused Iran of making up fake hits and doing everything to drive up oil prices before the U.S. midterm elections.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio remarked that shipping traffic across the Strait of Hormuz is returning to pre-war levels with more vessels crossing the strait.

However, the IRGC refuted the claims and observed that a few ships travelling during nighttime under the cover of darkness could not be construed as opening of the strait.

Energy traders are concerned that any renewal of military operations between the U.S. and Iran could disrupt the recent gradual rebound seen in oil flows out of the Arab region.

Besides this, the intense attacks by the Iran-aligned Houthi militia of Yemen against Saudi Arabia added to the Middle East concerns. Houthis claimed attacking Saudi Arabia's defense headquarters in Riyadh.

After Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports and other energy infrastructures, oil major Aramco of Saudi Arabia instructed its staff to evacuate Dhahran headquarters.

The Saudi-led coalition announced that its air defense systems intercepted and destroyed Houthi missiles that targeted Saudi Arabia.

Energy markets are also awaiting the upcoming announcement on interest rates by the U.S. Federal Reserve on Wednesday.

Crude oil being a dollar-denominated commodity, a change in interest rates could impact dollar value and consequently influence oil prices.

The U.S. dollar index was last seen trading at 101.82, up by 0.22 (or 0.22%) today.

data.title: Wolters Kluwer launches agentic tax preparation in CCH Axcess, the agentic platform for tax and accounting
data.description:
Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting today announced the launch of agentic tax return preparation in CCH Axcess™ Tax, further advancing CCH Axcess as the agentic platform for tax and accounting. Built into the cloud-native platform where firms already manage their tax work, agentic tax preparation helps firms reduce repetitive preparation work, increase capacity, and give tax professionals a stronger starting point for review.

For individual Form 1040 returns, CCH Axcess Tax powered by Expert AI prepares and calculates the return, then flags the exceptions that need attention before professional review begins. Firms can get more returns ready for review, while tax professionals remain in control of decisions and focus more of their time on judgment and client service.

“CCH Axcess is the agentic platform for tax and accounting, redefining the experience for both professionals and their clients,” said Cathy Rowe, Executive Vice President and Segment Leader, U.S. Professional Market, Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting. “Agentic tax preparation marks a significant shift in how tax work gets done. It helps firms create more capacity without sacrificing quality or control, so professionals can focus their expertise where it matters most.”

From manual preparation to focused review

Tax professionals traditionally spend significant time gathering documents, entering information, and checking work before review can begin. Unlike tools that automate a single task, agentic tax preparation in CCH Axcess Tax coordinates that work across multiple steps of the return process. Using prior-year information and current source documents, it can:

  • Identify expected documents and missing information

  • Classify documents and extract supported tax data

  • Map information into the return and calculate results

  • Surface diagnostics, review findings, and exceptions

  • Link calculated amounts to supporting evidence

  • Record decisions and generate workpapers for handoff

Firms get a clearer view of which returns are ready for review and what exceptions still need attention. Professionals review the work, resolve the issues requiring judgment, and retain responsibility for deciding and approving the final return.

Built into CCH Axcess, where work gets done

In CCH Axcess, agentic capabilities are built into the platform rather than separate products. Agentic tax preparation works inside CCH Axcess Tax, where the return is prepared, calculated and reviewed, connecting supported work from source documents through preparation, calculation, review and handoff.

Firms already collect client documents, extract data, manage workflow and identify advisory opportunities in CCH Axcess. That means Expert AI agents can move work forward using the firm’s own data, authoritative CCH content, and each firm’s permissions and controls. Expert AI agents prepare, check and advance the work. Professionals review, decide and approve.

Wolters Kluwer will share more about how CCH Axcess moves work forward across tax, planning and audit at CCH Connections 2026, beginning October 26 in Orlando.

For more information, visit the CCH Axcess Tax website.

data.title: ONGC Names Sunil Kumar Chairman For Three-year Tenure From 7 December
data.description:
The executive director will succeed Arun Singh, who has led the state-run oil and gas explorer since December 2022, as the company looks to boost domestic production and expand into energy transition

The Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) has approved Sunil Kumar's appointment as chairman of Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) for a combined tenure of three years, beginning 7 December, 2026.

Kumar, currently an executive director at ONGC, will assume charge on or after December 7 and serve until his superannuation in December 2028. His tenure will subsequently be extended on a contractual basis to complete the three-year term.

He will succeed Arun Singh, who has served as Chairman and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the state-run oil and gas explorer since December 2022.

Kumar's name was recommended for the top position following two rounds of interviews conducted by a search-cum-selection committee of the petroleum ministry. He will be the first ONGC Chairman to be elevated to the position from the executive director rank.

A petroleum engineering graduate of the Indian School of Mines, Dhanbad, Kumar, 58, also holds a postgraduate qualification in business management, specialising in marketing and finance. He took charge as executive director and asset manager of ONGC's Mehsana Asset in January 2025.

Focus On Production And Energy Transition

The leadership transition comes as ONGC faces pressure to increase domestic oil and gas production while diversifying into emerging areas of the energy transition.

The company accounts for 75 per cent of India's domestic crude oil and natural gas production, making its output performance significant for the country's efforts to strengthen domestic energy supplies.
